posts.title: Microsoft CppCon 2026 Trip Report
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
CppCon 2026 is a wrap! Microsoft returned to Aurora, Colorado, for a week of talks, technical discussions, and conversations with developers from across the C++ community.
Microsoft C++ @ CppCon
At our booth, we met people building games, financial systems, developer tools, embedded software, scientific tools, and other applications. Some were working with the latest language features, and others were maintaining and modernizing systems that have been in production for decades. Many talked to us about debugging, performance, build systems, or modern C++, and a growing number were experimenting with ways AI can help them accomplish their goals in the most effective way possible.
Attendees who completed our annual Microsoft C++ survey were entered for our daily LEGO raffle. This year’s prizes included some great LEGO sets; a retro gaming console, a retro camera, a mini orchid, and a model of the Milky Way galaxy.
Congratulations to our raffle winners and thank you to everyone who took the time to share detailed feedback.

Our Talks
I didn’t get a chance to attend many sessions as I spent most of my time talking with folks at the booth, but I was lucky enough to get to see most of our Microsoft sessions as they were being developed.
The Journey to “/W4 /WX”: How Hard Could It Be?

Keith Stockdale, from Rare, presented another session in his series of talks on dealing with the sometimes massive fallout from making small changes to your build system. After first establishing why someone should increase their warning level and treat warnings as errors, Keith walked through the diagnostics that show up, and how they were resolved.
And there were THOUSANDS of warnings, many of them previously suppressed through #pragmas or on the command line. Notably, the one warning that seemed to be the most pervasive was C4189 (local variable is initialized but not referenced) which they took from nearly 10,000 unique warnings down to zero! Definitely check this talk out if you are interested in generally improving the quality of your codebase and keeping your sanity intact while doing so.
C++ in the Age of AI: How Visual Studio Is Evolving

David Li and Augustin Popa presented this year’s version of our “what’s new” session for Visual Studio. GitHub Copilot has become an important part of the modern development toolbox, so much of the session was focused on how those features show up in Visual Studio, including AI workflows to modernize your code, reduce your build times, and debug your projects.
But there were plenty of features and improvements that aren’t specific to AI workflows, as well. Navigating your code in Visual Studio is now much faster with the latest versions, and MSVC Build Tools v14.52 (ships in November, release candidate available now) will ship with all C++23 features implemented and a /std:c++23 switch, which will also be compatible with C++/CLI. The team has also fixed nearly 650 bugs across the compiler, libraries, and IDEs since last year’s conference.
What’s New for C++ in Visual Studio Code: C++ and AI Tooling for Your Build, Your Code, Your Workflow
Watch it on YouTube!

Sinem Akinci and Ben McMorran gave a rundown on the latest and greatest for C++ users of Visual Studio Code. Our Visual Studio Code users are at the forefront of the AI agentic shift, and a lot of this session focused on how you can easily shift between different agentic experiences, depending on the nature of the work, and how you can customize your AI experience with Bring Your Own Key (BYOK), skills, custom agents, and hooks.
I tend to be a Visual Studio guy so a lot of this information wasn’t as useful to me in my day-to-day, but it was nice to see how excited Visual Studio Code users were to talk about their experiences with all of these new features. I for one am looking forward to the day when all AI tools have an easy-to-use BYOK experience that lets you run LLM inference on local hardware.
Turbocharging Native Code Performance: Compiler Optimization, Profile-guided Optimizations, and Beyond

I did get to spend some time in Eric Brumer’s session on how modern CPUs work, how to use profilers, and how those profiles can be used to optimize your products based on behavior of real users. Sample-based Profile Guided Optimizations (SPGO) is a pretty cool evolution of traditional Profile Guided Optimizations (PGO) and it’s already been deployed inside Microsoft to gain non-trivial runtime performance gains.
If you use C++ for the performance it unlocks for your applications, definitely catch this one when it’s available.
The C++ Safety Issues Your Tools Can’t See

Safety for C++ products has been a hot topic over the past decade, and there have been lots of papers and talks on the topic. Ion Todirel’s session starts by summarizing where we have been and introducing a way to discuss the different meanings of safety and how real issues map to them. One of the biggest points that I love to reinforce any chance I get, is that C++ is not C. Many of the problems that C++ has are things that it gets from its history of C compatibility, but unlike C, C++ has a long history of introducing features that are explicitly meant to avoid many of those problems. The talk closes out with a discussion about the broad solution space available to us and how AI can help us make our software safer.
My Major Takeaways
C++ Language Developments
Folks are really excited for new C++ language features, particularly reflection. There were already a couple of sessions, based on existing reflection implementations, showing really compelling things that can be done with the feature. It has the potential to be as impactful as templates were in how we write C++ code.
Performance is King
When we asked developers what they enjoy about C++, they often started with performance and control. CppCon attendees described building low-latency systems, game engines, embedded software, databases, compilers, infrastructure, scientific applications, and other software where memory use, hardware behavior, and predictable performance matter. They value the ability to choose a zero-cost abstraction when one fits, and to choose writing at a lower level when a problem requires it.
AI Normalization
The past few years have seen LLM-based AI workflows become increasingly common for attendees. It feels like there’s been a significant shift in the past year where people have really started to understand how they can use existing AI tools to complete their work faster and easier. Multiple attendees we talked to had conference badges that said something along the line of, “I haven’t written code in N months.” Folks are exploring new product surfaces, such as agentic CLI experiences and mostly-automated agents. There also seems to be much less friction getting started with AI tools, especially as products introduce BYOK capabilities and AI tools get approved for sensitive environments like restricted and air-gapped networks. I expect more talks on how to effectively use AI tools for C++ users in the coming years.
Thank you, CppCon
CppCon is valuable because it brings together people working on very different software who still share many of the same engineering questions.
How can we understand a large codebase more effectively? How can we improve performance without making code harder to maintain? How can we adopt a new language feature safely? Where can AI remove repetitive work, and where does an experienced developer need to stay closely involved?
Thank you to everyone who attended a Microsoft session, visited the booth, completed the survey, participated in an interview, or shared a project with us. Those conversations help us understand your workflows and pain points, and they help us improve the tools you use to make all those awesome products in C++.
CppCon is adding the 2026 session recordings to its video archive on a rolling basis. You can also follow the CppCon YouTube channel and the Microsoft C++ Team Blog for new videos, companion posts, and product updates.
We look forward to continuing the conversation.

posts.title: PrivacyLib: Privacy Controls at the Data Access Boundary
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
This latest deep dive into Meta’s Privacy Aware Infrastructure (PAI) takes a look at PrivacyLib. 
A privacy requirement must hold as data moves through Meta’s diverse data and processing systems. Historically, supporting a new requirement meant implementing the same enforcement logic separately in each system. PrivacyLib replaces this with a common library that runs inside the clients of Meta’s data and processing systems.
A system integrates with PrivacyLib once, and new privacy capabilities plug in as modules that reuse that integration. PrivacyLib performs billions of checks every second, and changes are simulated and rolled out per module. 
For internal AI agents, whose data access paths may not be known in advance, tool calls on supported paths carry agent context to PrivacyLib. The propagated context links each access to its session, so modules can observe data use and block operations that are not allowed.
At Meta, many privacy requirements ultimately come down to the same question: Can we prove that a piece of data goes only where it is allowed? At Meta’s scale, rather than relying solely on manual privacy audits, which can go out of sync as systems change, we have developed Privacy Aware Infrastructure (PAI) to answer this question within the infrastructure itself. PAI offers efficient and reliable first-class privacy constructs embedded in Meta’s infrastructure so that products can keep evolving quickly.
In previous posts, we have covered how data understanding, data lineage, and Policy Zones (our information flow control technology) play a role in PAI. Now, we are diving deep into PrivacyLib, a common library that runs inside the clients of hundreds of our data and processing systems at the point of data access.
PrivacyLib plays an important role in the final stage of the broader PAI workflow: continuously enforcing and monitoring data flows.
This blog post focuses on PrivacyLib’s role in the final stage of the PAI workflow.
Before PrivacyLib, we integrated privacy enforcement separately into the clients of each data and processing system for each requirement. With this approach, implementing a new requirement across systems could take months. Each new requirement, whether purpose limitation or data flow discovery, needed the same set of capabilities: covering a wide range of systems; deploying in weeks rather than months; running on every data access without becoming a latency problem; and rolling out enforcement changes without taking the fleet down. Over time, this approach became harder to scale as requirements and systems evolved.
PrivacyLib separates system integration from requirement implementation. We integrate each system once. When a requirement can be met at the point of data access, we implement it as a PrivacyLib module shared across the systems already integrated, so a new requirement no longer needs a separate implementation in each system. 
There are two kinds of modules: 
Enforcing modules can block a data access. For example, Policy Zones enforces purpose limitation.
Observing modules only record a data access. For example, Privacy Probes collects the runtime signals used to discover data flows. 
As internal AI agents became a new way of accessing data, we also added the Agent Observability module to observe agent-related data access events and help safeguard the data that agents can reach. Systems already integrated with PrivacyLib picked it up without new integration work, which is what integrating once buys: each new privacy capability arrives as a module, not as a project.
PrivacyLib replaces repeated implementations across systems.
Engineering Challenges and Approaches of PrivacyLib at Meta’s Scale
PrivacyLib operates across a broad range of data access paths at Meta:
More than a hundred libraries used to access data services, from key/value stores to AI features.
Thousands of production services with versions of the deployed library.
Millions of assets being accessed daily.
Billions of checks every second.
Operating at this scale creates three engineering challenges:
Challenge
Approach


Coverage: Systems can have multiple client libraries and legacy integrations, accept direct network calls, and offer direct database access to backing stores. All of them need to be handled to ensure requirements hold no matter the access path.
We integrate at two levels: typed client libraries, where PrivacyLib has full request context, and lower network boundaries on remaining RPC paths to get full coverage. Each integrated system maps its native APIs to PrivacyLib’s common operations and provides the inputs required by its configured modules. Once those pieces are in place, the same module can be enabled in multiple systems without a separate system-specific integration.


Scale: At billions of checks per second, even a small per-check computational cost becomes consequential across the fleet. Every service in the hot path pays that cost.
We compile requirements at build time into their simplest evaluable form and answer most checks from caches inside the process, so the common path avoids a network call.


Reliability: Privacy logic runs in the hot path of critical systems, owned by teams that release on their own schedules. A change has to be testable in isolation and reversible on its own, because a fleet-wide rollback cannot be the recovery path.
Enforcement is deployed as part of the service that owns it, so a change reaches production through that service’s own pipeline instead of a fleet-wide config push.





To illustrate how everything comes together at Meta’s scale, let’s walk through a privacy requirement that needs to be upheld when processing messaging metadata.
Users exchange messages through apps like Messenger, which supports end-to-end encryption. As Messenger routes and delivers those messages, subject to applicable law, its backend systems process non-content messaging data (i.e., messaging metadata), such as information about when messages are sent or delivered, to improve product performance, detect abuse, and protect users from harmful conduct. 
A variety of these backend services use Logger, a client library that runs in the service process, to write this metadata to data warehouse tables. Before writing a record, the PrivacyLib integration inside Logger invokes Policy Zones, an enforcing module, to check whether the metadata may flow to the destination table. This check is broken down into two parts: what inputs need to be available to make a decision, and how the check is actually evaluated at runtime. After examining these two parts, we look at how PrivacyLib scales across systems and how changes roll out without disrupting the services in the path.
PrivacyLib runs inside Logger’s client in the messaging backend service. It combines the request context with the generated destination metadata, invokes the modules configured for the write, and returns the enforcement decision to Logger.
Annotating Messaging Metadata
Every Logger destination table has a LoggerConfig that describes the records written to it. MetadataTraceLoggerConfig defines one such configuration for message-delivery traces and marks it as containing messaging metadata:
final class MetadataTraceLoggerConfig extends LoggerConfigBase {
  use MessagingTrafficMetadataPolicyTrait;
  public function configure(
    LoggerFieldDefiner $fd,
  ): LoggerFieldDefiner {
    $this->annotateWithTableLevelPolicy();
    // Field and destination definitions
  }
}
A logging destination can have many writers, so the annotation describing its output data belongs to the destination rather than to each service that writes to it. If every service declared the annotation separately, the declarations could disagree, or a new writer could omit it entirely. Declaring it once in LoggerConfig gives every writer the same description of the data.
For this destination, MessagingTrafficMetadataPolicyTrait supplies the MESSAGING_TRAFFIC_METADATA table-level annotation, and annotateWithTableLevelPolicy() attaches it to the destination.
LoggerConfig is Logger’s own schema, and each system describes its data in its own format. To give PrivacyLib a single form to consume, Logger’s code-generation pipeline translates the configuration into a PrivacyLib-compatible artifact. The generated MetadataTraceLoggerConfigPrivacyLibArtifact is derived from MetadataTraceLoggerConfig and carries the destination identity and the messaging annotation:
/**
 * @codegen-source MetadataTraceLoggerConfig
 */
class MetadataTraceLoggerConfigPrivacyLibArtifact
  extends LoggerInputPrivacyLibArtifact {
  
  final public static function getAssetIDImpl(
  ): LoggerInputAssetID {
    return LoggerInputAssetID::get(
      'MetadataTraceLoggerConfig',
    );
  }

  protected static function getPurposePolicyVars(
  ): TPurposePolicyVars {
    return PurposePolicy::makeVars(
      TPurposePolicyName::MESSAGING_TRAFFIC_METADATA,
    );
  }

  // Other generated fields omitted.
}
The generated class above is used by Logger’s client in Hack, Meta’s typed PHP language. For its C++ and Python clients, Logger publishes destination identities and annotations to a central catalog. PrivacyLib uses that information to generate language-specific artifacts. In the C++ example in the next section, PrivacyLib uses the LoggerConfig name to load the C++ artifact for the destination.  
Running the Check
The artifact from the previous section describes one Logger destination. PrivacyLib also needs to know what a Logger write means and which modules should run. Logger’s Hack integration defines that once for all destinations:
$config->libraryConfig()->enablePrivacyLib(
  PrivacyLibOperation::write()
    ->input(
      PrivacyLibInput::instance(
        nameof ILoggerInputPrivacyLibPayloadProvider,
      ),
    )
    ->enforcements(
      PrivacyLibWriteEnforcement::zones(
        ZoneDataType::LOGGER,
      )
        ->withPropagation()
        ->enabled(),
      PrivacyLibWriteEnforcement::telemetryLogging()->enabled(),
      // Other modules
    ),
);
PrivacyLibOperation::write() declares PrivacyLib’s write operation for Logger, and enforcements() lists the modules that run on it. The Policy Zones module can affect the result, while the Telemetry Logging module records the evaluation without affecting it. Adding a module here requires no changes to individual destinations or Logger call sites. ZoneDataType::LOGGER tells Policy Zones that it is checking a Logger destination.
In C++ services, Logger constructs the PrivacyLib request as follows: 
const auto assetList =
      std::vector<std::string>{configName};

PrivacyLibBuilder builder(
      "LOGGER_WRITE_CLIENT",
      assetList,
      LoggerWriteAPIEnumHelper::apiToHashedString(
          PolicyEnforcedLoggerWriteAPI::log),
      Caller::LOGGER,
      getLoggerWriteImplementation());

auto result =
      PrivacyLibRequest(std::move(builder)).dispatch();

PrivacyLib uses configName to load the destination’s artifact. The hashed PolicyEnforcedLoggerWriteAPI::log value maps Logger’s API to PrivacyLib’s write operation. The remaining builder arguments identify Logger as the caller and provide the implementation that performs the write. dispatch() invokes the configured modules and records their outcomes. For the Policy Zones module, PrivacyLib provides the destination annotations from the generated artifact and the current processing context. For this example, Policy Zones evaluates two conditions:
The current context represents an allowed use of messaging metadata.
The destination artifact carries the MESSAGING_TRAFFIC_METADATA annotation.
When enforcement is enabled, the Policy Zones module denies the write if either condition fails. PrivacyLib combines the results from enforcing modules into one response. A denial stops the write before Logger sends the record downstream. Observing modules emit telemetry without affecting the response.
A closer look at module evaluation on a Logger write.
Scaling Privacy Checks Across Systems
PrivacyLib enables privacy checks to scale across heterogeneous systems through a common execution model, lightweight evaluation and telemetry, and coverage for requests that bypass integrated clients. 
A Common Execution Model Across Systems
PrivacyLib’s integrations span systems with very different APIs: key-value stores, graph databases, ML pipelines, filesystems, and logging systems like Logger. Each integration maps its access points to one of five common operations, and PrivacyLib invokes its modules at each:
Read: runs when fetching data.
Write: runs when storing data.
RPC: runs when calling another service.
Request entry: runs once when a service begins handling a request.
Inline execution: wraps a specific computation inside a larger request, such as evaluating a feature. Data accesses made during that computation are evaluated using its inline privacy context.
Modules are written against these five operations rather than against each system’s native API. Reads, writes, and RPCs also have post-operation variants, so observing modules can run after the access decision has been made. Once a system provides the mapping, every compatible module can reuse it, which is why enabling an additional module on an already-integrated system takes only days.
PrivacyLib runs inside the clients of data and processing systems because the clients already have the destination identity and request context that modules need. Keeping the evaluation in the same process avoids carrying those inputs across process boundaries on every access. This design also has two advantages:
Richer context: PrivacyLib can use the caller’s identity, endpoint, and purpose while that information is still available. This information is frequently lost if the check is evaluated on the datastore.
Failure isolation: A faulty change is contained to the service running that version of the code, keeping the shared datastore outside the failure boundary.
Keeping Checks Computationally Inexpensive
In-process evaluation must also be computationally efficient because it runs on every data access. Per-request caches eliminate repeated checks within a request and per-host caches retain frequently used configuration and results. This avoids the remote configuration fetch required by an earlier design (that fetch alone was thousands of times slower than the in-process path). The result is that PrivacyLib performs billions of checks per second across the fleet with low per-check latency, while consuming only a small fraction of Meta’s total compute capacity.
At PrivacyLib’s scale, telemetry must also remain lightweight. PrivacyLib records each module’s status, samples latency, and logs errors, giving us fleet-wide visibility into how enforcement is behaving in production. Recording every invocation in full detail would overwhelm the systems receiving those events, so the goal is to deduplicate repeated events while keeping rare ones visible. 
Two mechanisms work together to achieve this: Bloom filters on each host downsample high-volume patterns at a fixed rate, and fine-grained sampling rates adjust as traffic changes.
Covering Direct RPC Paths
Not every caller accesses data through a PrivacyLib-integrated client library; some issue raw RPCs. The RPC layer can still check those requests, but it sees far less context than the client does. PrivacyLib bridges that gap with a cryptographically-signed token: When a client-side check succeeds, PrivacyLib attaches the token to the request, and ServiceRouter validates it at a lower boundary for supported RPC traffic, confirming that the request already passed the richer client-side check.
When a request arrives at the RPC layer without a token, ServiceRouter falls back to a coarser check based only on the context visible in the network payload. Because that context is limited, the lower layer applies the strictest interpretation, choosing false positives over gaps. Between them, the two layers cover access through Meta-managed clients and supported RPC paths. Paths outside those boundaries are not covered by this mechanism and need their own PrivacyLib integration.
Together, the result is that evaluation stays local and computationally inexpensive wherever possible, with a coarser backstop where local evaluation is unavailable, and modules have one place to run across systems that otherwise share nothing. What remains is the harder operational question: how to change enforcement behavior without breaking live traffic or making incorrect access decisions.
Rolling Out Enforcement Changes Safely
Privacy requirements change over time. Updates to a destination’s annotation or an enforcing module can change whether a write is allowed. PrivacyLib has a safe rollout path for both types of changes.
Changing an Annotation
Adding or removing an annotation changes two lines in a LoggerConfig: the declaration that imports MessagingTrafficMetadataPolicyTrait and the call to annotateWithTableLevelPolicy(). Because the destination may have many writers, that two-line edit can begin blocking writes from many services at once.
Review is therefore built around showing the author and reviewers what the edit will actually do. During code review, Logger’s code-generation pipeline updates the destination’s PrivacyLib artifact. Simulations then replay observed data flows against both the new artifact and the existing one, and any flow whose result changes is reported. The source edit, the generated artifact, and the simulation results are reviewed together, so the decision rests on evidence of the change’s effect rather than only on reading the code change. If the simulation reports an unexpected change, reviewers hold the artifact before release.

Once approved, the artifact reaches services through their usual build and deployment pipeline. That gives two forms of visibility before the change is deployed, from the decision changes reported by the simulation and the generated code showing exactly what will be deployed, plus one form of control, since each service’s own deployment decides when the change reaches production. It also bounds the surface area: An issue found after deployment is limited to the services running that build.
The downside is that changes do not reach the entire fleet at once, making change propagation slower than a global configuration update. In practice, requirement owners use explicit tracking to update the services in scope by the required deadline, while a service that needs the update sooner can use its emergency deployment process.
Simulation reveals decision changes before release, while independent service deployments control timing to limit production impact.
Rolling Out a Module
An annotation change applies to one Logger destination. A module added to Logger’s write path runs for every Logger destination. We therefore deploy the module before enabling it across all traffic.
As an example, here is how Policy Zones was introduced on this path. We first set the Policy Zones module to rollingOut() in Logger’s PrivacyLib write-operation configuration:
PrivacyLibWriteEnforcement::zones(ZoneDataType::LOGGER)
    ->rollingOut()
The rollout key, logger.input.write.zones, identified this combination of Logger input, write operation and the Policy Zones module. rollingOut() placed the module execution behind a runtime control. We then moved that control from 0 to 100% in stages while monitoring denials, errors, and latency. If valid writes began to fail, we could lower the percentage without rebuilding or redeploying the service. The Telemetry Logging module continues to run because it is configured independently. 
Once the Policy Zones module was stable across Logger traffic, we changed the configuration from rollingOut() to enabled(). At this point, the Logger integration ran the module without consulting the rollout percentage.
After deployment, engineers use runtime signals to increase, reduce, or stop a module rollout without rebuilding or redeploying.
Safeguards apply at different stages across the two change paths described above. If a simulation shows unexpected flow changes, we hold the annotation artifact before release. If a module misbehaves after the rollout begins, we lower its rollout percentage using the runtime control.
These safety mechanisms changed what it takes to meet a privacy requirement at Meta. PrivacyLib now runs inside the clients of hundreds of data and processing systems and evaluates billions of checks every second, while consuming a small fraction of Meta’s compute. Requirements built on top of it, such as purpose limitation through Policy Zones and data flow discovery through Privacy Probes, reuse those integrations instead of rebuilding them, so enabling a module on systems that are already covered takes days rather than the months bespoke integrations used to take. When a change does go wrong, the failure stays inside the service running the deployed change. We can now use that foundation for a newer class of workload: AI agents.
PrivacyLib Controls for AI Agents
AI agents are harder to reason about than traditional services because their behavior is dynamic and the data they access is determined at runtime. Therefore, we have to design for agent safety up front by enforcing controls, such as Policy Zones, not only on what we expected the agents to access when we built them but also on what they attempt to access at runtime. Where enabled, these controls can block a disallowed access before any data is returned.
Agents invoke tools to carry out tasks. A single tool call may cross several services in a nested manner before reaching data. To tackle this new challenge, we built AgentLib, a common runtime based on PrivacyLib’s design principles, for observing and governing tool calls made by internal agents. On supported paths, AgentLib associates each tool call with its agent session, and downstream clients and services propagate that context until the call reaches a system integrated with PrivacyLib. At that data access boundary, PrivacyLib combines the context, the requested operation, and the destination’s annotations, then passes them to individual modules to make a final decision.
Within PrivacyLib, the Agent Observability module records the agent session and tool-call identifiers alongside the destination, client API, integration point, and any errors. Engineers can query these events by session to investigate the services and destinations involved in a tool call. When we introduced the Agent Observability module, PrivacyLib’s existing broad coverage enabled us to instrument systems already integrated with the library instead of manually integrating the module into hundreds of systems. Even with AI-assisted development, this would have been a daunting task. 
To enforce certain policies, we used the existing Policy Zones module without modification because it relies on the same inputs for enforcement. On paths where this control is enabled, it considers the destination annotations and agent context before allowing an operation. When Policy Zones blocks an operation, PrivacyLib propagates that result back through the call chain to the agent environment. Policy Zones applies this check even when the agent chooses a tool that its developer did not anticipate. The access decision does not depend on the agent behaving as intended.
AgentLib associates supported tool calls made by internal agents with agent context, which services propagate to PrivacyLib at the data access boundary. PrivacyLib uses that context for observation and enforcement.
Lessons Learned From Building and Operating PrivacyLib
Building and operating PrivacyLib across Meta’s systems taught us a few important lessons.
Design for evolving systems and requirements: Before PrivacyLib, we added privacy controls to the individual call sites needed to satisfy each new requirement. Over time, Meta built new data and processing systems, services gained new ways to process data, and privacy requirements expanded. Each change created more integration work, and new access paths sometimes appeared faster than we could cover them. The lesson was to integrate at a stable data access boundary, define the small set of operations that systems share, and keep annotations with the data. Modules can reuse the same integrations and reduce engineering effort over time.
Reliability earns adoption: Early on, an invalid config crashed processes across the fleet, breaking our own safe rollout principles. Other incidents came from annotation changes that compiled successfully but changed access decisions and caused product failures. These incidents showed that service owners will trust PrivacyLib in a critical data access path only when they can see how changes affect their traffic before release and recover from a problematic change without a fleet-wide rollback. 
Coverage includes deployment: When new requirements need changes to modules or supported policies and annotations, older services need to deploy versions with the updated PrivacyLib capabilities. We have ensured that explicit inventory, tracking, and rollout mechanisms are in place to coordinate these deployments, so that requirement owners can meet deadlines safely by updating only the services in scope.
Looking Forward
These lessons shape where we are taking PrivacyLib next, as AI pushes data access into environments and call paths that are increasingly novel. We continue to enrich PrivacyLib’s capabilities in two areas:
AI training: Data used for training reaches our systems from a variety of environments. Much of it is produced or transformed in various places. We are extending PrivacyLib-style approaches to this domain so the same guarantees scale with it. For more on how Meta approaches AI training data, see AI at Meta: Transparency About Our Training Data.
Internal AI agents: Observing attempted data accesses and blocking disallowed ones is just the starting point rather than a finished picture for agents used internally at Meta for engineering and productivity. The harder problems come next: evaluating internal agent behavior while it is happening, and reasoning about communication between these agents, where a single data access may be several agents removed from the person who asked for it.
Acknowledgements
The authors would like to acknowledge the contributions of many current and former Meta employees who have played a crucial role in developing PrivacyLib over the years. In particular, we would like to extend special thanks to (in alphabetical order) Adwait Sathe, Andrew Vaslas, Darrien Glasser, Diana Marsala, Hanzhi Zhang, Kousik Nandy, Matthew Hillman, Matthieu Martin, Michael Dietz, Nathan Maue, Ramy Wassef, Sen Luo, Spencer Baumgardner, Vince Yang, and Zhong Hu. We would also like to express our gratitude to all reviewers of this post, including (in alphabetical order) Aleksandar Ilic, Alex Kagan, Alex Ponomarenko, Arash Nikkar, Avtar Brar, Chloe Lu, Chris Wiltz, Emil Vazquez, Emily Van Deuren, Rituraj Kirti, Sushaant Mujoo, and Wenlong Dong. posts.title: Python Typing Survey 2026: AI Tools and the Shifting Checker Landscape
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
The 2026 Python Typing Survey received 1,794 responses. 
Type hint use changed little across three years, but checker selection changed sharply. 
Among respondents who reported which checkers they use, half selected more than one, and missing library type information was the most common difficulty.
For the third consecutive year, we asked Python developers how they use and experience Python typing: the language features, specifications, and tools used to describe and check types in Python code. We run the survey to learn what is working and what library maintainers, tool builders, documentation authors, and standards contributors should tackle next.
Most respondents were experienced Python developers: 76.4% had used Python for at least five years. The clearest change was the shift in checker choice, while missing library type information remained the most common difficulty.
Key Takeaways From the 2026 Python Typing Survey
This year’s findings show several recurring opportunities: 
Broader and more accurate type information would help users of data-science packages: Dynamic frameworks pose a different challenge because current type systems cannot express some runtime behavior. Possible directions include new typing features and checker support tailored to individual libraries and frameworks.
Tool builders could focus on editor feedback and an initial checker run that requires little configuration: Error messages could link to short explanations and examples. Typing documentation can assume Python experience. Projects using multiple checkers would benefit from clear explanations of intentional differences between them.
Better callable syntax remains a practical area for standards work, especially if improvements keep common typing tasks straightforward.
AI usage remains an open question: The findings on AI leave an open question about which interactions between AI tools and type checkers help developers. Further empirical study could inform future designs.
AI Tools Now Write Types and Respond to Checker Errors
The share of respondents who selected “Makes AI-generated code more accurate/reliable” rose from 18.5% in 2025 to 38.4% in 2026. AI tools wrote type hints for 42.5% of 1,517 respondents, while 32.6% wrote types to improve AI-generated code. Respondents also used AI to fix or explain type errors. Across all four activities listed for AI tool use in typing, 61.0% of respondents reported they used at least one of these options.
Some respondents said their AI coding tool runs the checker and then fixes the errors. Of the 1,517 developers who answered how they run a checker, 24.4%, said an AI coding tool invoked their checker. Among the 370 respondents, 61.6% also used AI to fix checker errors. The rate was 19.3% among everyone else.
Some respondents described AI-generated types that are too broad and agents that suppress checker errors:
“I fix AI coded type hints because AI often gets lazy and uses object for everything.”


“Lazy coding agents that spam #type: ignore comments everywhere.”

When asked how useful types are for better AI-assisted coding, 29.8% of 1,551 respondents chose “I’m not sure.” The uncertainty rate for AI-assisted coding was nearly four times the 7.7% rate for runtime guarantees, the next-highest of the six benefits. We still need empirical evidence about which interactions actually help.
The Pyrefly team is already studying how AI coding tools and type checkers work together. At the 2026 Python Typing Summit, the team presented Type Checking in Agentic Workflows.
Library Gaps Lead Overall; Occasional Users Struggle With Complexity
Missing type information in third-party libraries was the leading difficulty, selected by 65.1% of 1,486 respondents. Another 44.6% said the type system could not describe everything their code does.
Developers can still have a poor experience after a library ships dedicated stubs. Among 156 people who wrote their own answer, 22 described dynamic constructs, decorators, metaprogramming, or framework behavior. Ten described arrays, dataframes, or scientific typing, and at least eight described annotations that were inaccurate, incomplete, or too broad. Respondents repeatedly named Django, SQLAlchemy, Pydantic, NumPy, pandas, and Polars.
“Django does so much black magic it’s a wonder a type checker works at all.” — survey respondent

Library maintainers need annotations that capture how frameworks and data-science libraries behave. The Pyrefly team has been working with Quansight to improve third-party library typing, including contributions to pandas-stubs and NumPy.
Frequency of use changed which problems stood out. Among developers who used type hints rarely or sometimes, 41.6% found the type system too complex or verbose. The rate was 14.5% among developers who used type hints often or always. Missing library typing affected 36.2% of the lower-frequency group and 70.0% of the higher-frequency group.

“I use the straightforward parts and avoid the parts that are difficult to understand.” — survey respondent. 

Years of typing experience showed a different pattern. Complexity was reported by 18.2% of respondents with zero to two years of typing experience, 16.0% with three to six years, and 21.0% with seven or more. Newer typing users were often regular users and experienced Python developers: Of the 396 respondents with zero to two years of typing experience, 306 (77.3%) used type hints often or always and 345 (87.1%) had used Python for at least three years.
Guidance for developers who are new to typing should assume Python experience and show how to add types to an existing repository. Occasional users need a useful first check with little configuration and easy-to-understand errors. As we change the type system, we should aim to support more patterns without making common tasks harder.
Better Callable syntax is one practical place to start. It was the most selected missing feature, chosen by 45.7% of the 1,486 respondents who answered the question. The selection rate was similar for respondents who reported complexity and the rest of the sample.
Newer Checkers Gained Ground Quickly
Frequent type hint use remained between 85.5% and 88.0% across the three surveys: 88.0% in 2024, 85.9% in 2025, and 85.5% in 2026. A different group answered each year, but the overall rate remained consistent.

Checker choice was far less stable. When the 2024 Python Typing survey asked what feature was missing from the Python type system, one response now reads like a preview of the changes captured in this year’s results:
“A faster Mypy. Its lack of speed led to ecosystem fracturing and other type checkers don’t support Mypy plugins and behave differently in general.” – survey respondent

By 2026, developers had several newer open-source checkers to choose from. Speed or performance topped the reasons for choosing a checker, at 56.5%. Using the same list of checkers in both years, 49.9% selected two or more in 2026, up from 46.0% in 2025.
Pyrefly is developed by Meta. Respondents could select more than one checker, so the percentages may overlap.
Developers Mix Checkers Across Their Workflows
Of the 700 respondents who selected Mypy, 297 also selected its editor plugin. Another 314 selected a different named checker integration without selecting the Mypy plugin.
Most Pyrefly respondents also selected another checker: 220 of 264, or 83.3%. In the free-text responses, developers described why their teams divide work between checkers:
“Because my team members use different IDEs, we use multiple type checkers for development, but rely on Mypy for linting (local and CI).” — survey respondent
“Locally we primarily use Pyright because it’s the only option we’ve tried that fully understands all the more niche typing patterns within our codebase. In CI/CD, we do a Pyrefly run and only run Pyright on files where Pyrefly fails, to improve performance of the check.” — survey respondent 

Among the 1,486 developers who answered the question about difficulties, 33.3% reported inconsistencies between checkers. Among the 738 respondents who selected multiple static checkers and answered the difficulty question, 315 (42.7%) reported inconsistencies between checkers.
IDE Support Remains Central as Typing Help Moves Away From Stack Overflow
Readability or documentation was the most selected reason to use type hints, chosen by 93.6% of 1,571 respondents. Editor support also ranked highly: 84.8% of the 1,494 people who gave it a numeric rating chose 4 or 5. About 39% of the 103 developers who supplied their own reason mentioned completion, navigation, hover information, or editor error messages.
“Drastically improves IDE tooltip/autocomplete.” – survey respondent 

Real-time editor feedback was widespread: 82.9% of 1,517 respondents ran a type checker in an editor. VS Code was the most selected editor or IDE, at 59.3%.
Where developers look for help has changed as well. From 2024 to 2026, Stack Overflow use fell from 46.4% to 22.9%, while large language model (LLM) chat rose from 26.0% to 41.7%. Python typing documentation rose from 56.2% to 65.9%. Checker-specific documentation ended at 60.5%, up from 52.2% after a dip in 2025. General Python documentation fell from 66.7% to 62.2%.

As developers move from Stack Overflow to typing- and checker-specific documentation, the quality of those sources matters more. Error messages should link to short, relevant explanations and examples. Links to documentation would also give LLM chat tools better information to work with.
Survey Results and Raw Data
Download the full results and data from the Python Typing Survey 2026.
Acknowledgements
The survey ran from August 5 through September 2, 2026. It was developed with support from the Pyrefly team at Meta, the PyCharm team at JetBrains, the Python team at Microsoft, the ty team at Astral/OpenAI, and community contributors on discuss.python.org. We shared it through Reddit, X, Mastodon, newsletters, the Python typing forum, LinkedIn, Bluesky, Discord, Slack, and type-checker project websites and social accounts. We lightly edited quotations for spelling, grammar, and punctuation. We thank everyone who responded, shared the survey, reviewed the data, or contributed to the Python typing community.

posts.title: Meta Networking at the 2026 OCP Global Summit: Open Innovation for Scale-Up, Scale-Out, and Scale-Across AI Networks
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
At the 2026 Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit, Meta shared the networking innovations that are directly supporting our latest AI models, including Muse Wonder and Muse Spark, and our gigawatt-scale Prometheus cluster. 
Highlights
IcePack & IceCube: Meta’s first liquid-cooled network rack with 102.4T switch blades (128×800G, Broadcom Tomahawk 6C and NVIDIA Spectrum-6 variants), running FBOSS. 
Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF) for scale-out: Meta’s multi-plane scale-out fabric where each GPU connects to eight network planes. 3-tier → 2-tier Clos, NIC-level packet spraying, and a combined host+switch control plane. Built with NVIDIA and shared with our cloud partners.
Scale-across: BAG, our petabit-scale super-spine joining buildings, campuses, and regions in our gigawatt-scale Prometheus cluster, plus SRv6 regional backbones on FBOSS + SAI.
Ethernet for scale-up: Tahan, the Ethernet scale-up switch for MTIA 300 based on Broadcom Tomahawk5; a preview of 72 accelerators per rack on 102.4T silicon; and ESUN progressing from 1.0 → 1.1.
OSPA: a new OCP initiative co-led by Meta, Microsoft, and Alibaba to standardize the switch platform layer. v1.0 spec submitted to OCP.
MetaRoCE: our RDMA transport for AI networks, now going open source.
We shared insights into key networking-related initiatives through talks from many of the Meta network and hardware teams. Those talks and their slide decks are now available to everyone! 
Keynote and Executive Sessions

Concrete to Code: Engineering AI Infrastructure at Gigawatt Scale (video)
AI has changed the shape of infrastructure. Santosh Janardhan, Head of Infrastructure at Meta, shares how Meta is designing, building, and operating at a scale that requires rethinking the network, the facility, and the systems that hold it all together.
Speaker: Santosh Janardhan, Head of Infrastructure, Meta
Betting on the Network: Meta’s Case for Full-Stack, Open AI Networking (video)
 AI progress now depends on the network as much as on compute. The path forward is a full-stack, open approach built in the open ecosystem rather than behind proprietary walls.
Speaker: Omar Baldonado, Senior Director, Data Center & AI Networking, Meta
Breaking the Walls: Open Scale-Across for the AI Era (video)
Training compute is compounding faster than infrastructure can scale. This talk lays out why open scale-across networking is needed to connect AI capacity across data centers and regions.
Speakers: Vipul Deokar, VP, Core Network Infrastructure, Meta; Rakesh Chopra, SVP, Silicon & Systems Architecture and Engineering Fellow, Cisco; Tom Williams, VP, Marketing, Cisco
Switch Platforms, Optics, and Interconnect
Meta 102.4T Ethernet Switch (video)
IceCube is Meta’s 102.4T switch that goes into our liquid-cooled Icepack rack. Icecube and N-IceCube are based on a 2OU, hybrid liquid/air-cooled, PHY-less design and incorporate either the Broadcom Tomahawk 6C or NVIDIA Spectrum-6 ASICs with 128x800GE of non-blocking capacity.
Speakers: Rongchun Zhou, Network Hardware Engineer, Meta; Reza Niazmand, Network Technical Program Manager, Meta
Integrated Optics at Scale: From 51.2T CPO Validation to Meta’s 102.4T (video)
A look at why integrated optics matter for rack-scale AI — power, density, disaggregation, and reliability — and what Meta learned validating 51.2T co-packaged optics that could carry over to 102.4T.
Speakers: Granthana Rangaswamy, Hardware Engineer, Meta; Siamak Amiralizadeh, Optical Engineer, Meta; Xu Wang, Hardware Engineer, Meta
Operating Linear Pluggable Optics at Hyperscale (video)
At AI scale, the per-module retimer DSP is a repeated tax in power, heat, and cost across millions of links — but removing it moves equalization and triage onto the host. This talk answers whether linear optics can match retimed reliability at fleet scale.
Speakers: Amin Yekani, Optical Engineer, Meta; Qing Wang, Optical Engineer, Meta
Large-Scale Deployment of 800G AECs in Meta Data Centers (video)
The economics of AI networking are set at the short-reach link. This session covers Meta’s large-scale deployment of 800Gb/s active electrical cables and the component quality work behind it.
Speakers: Jingyu (Kevin) Yu, Component Quality Engineer, Meta; Abhijit Chakravarty, Quality Head, Optics & Interconnects, Meta
Beyond Pluggables: Building the NPO Ecosystem for Scaling AI
A look at what it takes to build a near-package optics (NPO) ecosystem capable of supporting AI scaling beyond what pluggable modules can deliver.
Speaker: Nan Ge, Technical Sourcing Manager, Meta 
FBOSS and Open Platforms

Open Switch Platform Architecture (OSPA) — A Unified Network Switch Platform Reference Design (video)
While SAI has made data plane software portable, the switch platform layer remains proprietary and fragmented, adding months of duplicated bring-up work per platform. This talk introduces OSPA, which proposes a unified, multi-vendor reference design for that layer, and the 1.0 specification that has been contributed to OCP.
Speakers: Tao Ren, Tian Fang, and Xu Wang, Meta; Guohan Lu, Individual; Ying Xie, Microsoft; Yiyuan Huang and Zhiping Yao, Alibaba
NVIDIA SDK + FBOSS: Building Production-Ready AI Network Fabrics (video)
How NVIDIA’s Spectrum-X switch, SDK, SAI implementation, and simulator come together with FBOSS, Meta’s network operating system, to build production AI fabrics. The talk covers the CI/CD and test-driven workflow that made rapid joint integration possible.
Speakers: Parvez Shaikh, Meta; Harish Krishnamoorthy, Alan Elder, and Tom Zhu, NVIDIA
Open, AI-Ready FBOSS: From Platform Bring-up to Solution Qualification (video)
A tour of the FBOSS software stack — routing, forwarding, platform services, and board support — and how a config-driven approach can more quickly and easily take a platform from board bring-up to qualified status for the OCP ecosystem.
Speakers: Srikrishna Gopu, Software Engineer, Meta; Benoit Sigoure, Software Engineer, Nexthop AI
Experiences With Scale-Out and Scale-Across
High Performance at Scale and Reliability by Design: Operating Meta’s Largest AI Clusters (video)
What it takes to operate Meta’s largest AI clusters reliably, walking the full training stack from GPUs and scale-up fabrics through FBOSS, drivers, communication libraries, and the scheduler.
Speakers: Jose Leitao, Production Engineering, Meta; Guille Cobo, Network.AI, Meta
Scaling AI Infrastructure Across DC and Beyond: Meta’s Journey with BAG (video)
An overview of Backend Aggregation (BAG) — its purpose, architecture, and performance benefits — with lessons from deployment in Meta’s Prometheus cluster. The talk also covers the engineering challenges of platform fit, distance management, reliability, and capacity planning, especially given the quickly evolving AI ecosystem.
Speakers: Jalpa Patel, Technical Program Manager, Meta; Hany Morsy, Network Engineer, Meta
SRv6 Powered Backbone Networks (video)
This talk delves into why Meta chose SRv6 for a new layer of its backbone, how the data plane and control plane work in production on FBOSS (including using shallow buffers at WAN distances), and the accelerated timeline from concept to deployment in a matter of months. 
 Speakers: Jasmeet Bagga, Software Engineer, Meta; Andrey Golovanov, Network Engineer, Meta
Bridging On-prem and Cloud: GPU Networking at Meta Scale (video)
A look at how Meta uses cloud GPU capacity, and what lessons Meta brings from its on-premises deployments into clouds to make them highly performant and reliable for AI workloads.
Speakers: Adi Gangidi, Technical Lead, Meta; Carmen Au, Software Engineering Manager, Meta
Scale-Across Networking Panel (video)
A cross-industry panel on what scale-across AI clusters demand from routing and optical transport equipment. Panelists compare approaches across hyperscalers, silicon, and systems vendors.
Panelists: Jeff Rahn, Meta; Tad Hofmeister, Google Cloud; Yawei Yin, Microsoft Azure; Xiguang (Henry) Wu, Broadcom; Vijay Vusirikala, Arista Networks (moderator)
Scale-Up and ESUN
Tahan: An Open, Ethernet-Based Scale-Up Switch for MTIA (video)
We introduce Tahan, an Ethernet-based scale-up switch for our rack-scale MTIA 300 AI system. This talk walks through Tahan’s bandwidth and latency characteristics and scale-up feature set, demonstrating Ethernet’s strengths in scale-up and moving toward ESUN for future scale-up designs.
Speakers: Vimal Vasudevan, Technical Program Manager, Meta; Ashutosh Grewal, Software Engineer, Meta
ESUN: Open Ethernet for the AI Scale-Up Era (video)
We partnered with the community last year to launch ESUN: Ethernet for Scale-up Networking. This talk covers progress since the last OCP Global Summit, with the 1.0 specification released earlier in the year and the upcoming 1.1 specification. 
Speakers: Manoj Wadekar, AI Network Technologist, Meta; Pratik Marolia, AI System Architect, Microsoft
Validation Methodologies for the ESUN Ecosystem (video)
A validation methodology for the ESUN ecosystem, situating scale-up within the broader set of AI scaling domains — scale in, up, out, across, edge, and above.
Speakers: Manoj Wadekar, AI Systems Technologist, Meta; Venkat Pullela, CTO, AI Infrastructure, Keysight
Test Methodology for Multi-Accelerator Copper Scale-up Interconnect (video)
In a copper scale-up domain, thousands of connections per rack mean roughly 10 bad links even at 99.9% yield — and blind-mate cartridges leave no per-link serviceability. At Meta, we look at this as a statistical problem rather than a set of isolated debugging problems. This talk shares our test methodology.
Speakers: Yao Rong, Systems Engineer, AI Systems, Meta; Karthik Ganesan, AI/HPC System Performance Engineer, Meta
RDMA Transport
MetaRoCE: Rethinking RDMA for AI (video)
The network is now in the critical path for AI clusters, with all-reduce and all-to-all performance gated by the slowest node across hundreds of thousands of accelerators. This talk covers the MetaRoCE transport specification.
Speakers: Arvind Srinivasan, Meta; Sandeep Nagaraja, Meta; Balakrishnan Raman, AMD
MetaRoCE in Software (video)
Meta is making its MetaRoCE software implementations available in open source, starting with a user-space version on GitHub (libsoftmetaroce) with a DPDK-based version coming soon. 
Speakers: Ashkan Nikravesh, Software Engineer, Meta; Yiorgos Nikolaidis, Software Engineer, Meta
Watch Everything From the 2026 OCP Global Summit 
You can watch all of the recorded talks from the event on the 2026 OCP Global Summit website.
A huge thank-you to every presenter from our Meta network and hardware teams and to our great partners across the industry who made this possible! 
Images courtesy Open Compute Project (OCP).

posts.title: Making Failure Diagnosis Reliable with Pensive AI
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
By Praneeth Yenugutala, Victor Dusa, Anastasia Samoilova, Megan Ren, Justin Wei, Marcelo Mayworm
At Netflix, data and machine learning practitioners run millions of workloads each day across orchestration systems and compute engines such as Titus, Spark, Trino, and Druid. On peak days, roughly 100,000 workloads fail. When workloads fail, the failure itself is only the beginning. Someone still needs to find the useful signal in several logs, decide whether the cause sits in their code or the platform, and determine whether to retry, reconfigure, or escalate. Even a small share of difficult failures can consume engineering time, waste compute, and interrupt critical data pipelines.
Our first answer to that problem was Pensive, an auto-diagnosis and remediation system in Netflix’s data platform. Pensive collected logs from failed workloads, used regular expressions and hand-authored Java rules to extract and classify errors, then passed retry or remediation guidance to products such as Maestro. It made ~ 50% of failures self-service and, in some cases, automatic.
Rules work well for known patterns, but their coverage grows only when someone recognizes a new failure mode, understands the logs, writes a rule, and keeps it current as engines and log formats change. Over one three-month period, Pensive processed roughly seven million job-failure classifications, yet about half fell into the unknown bucket. We needed a way to expand coverage without giving up the deterministic parts of Pensive that already worked.
To solve this ambiguous and complex problem at Netflix scale, we invested in Pensive AI to add AI-assisted error extractions and focused diagnosis and remediation guidance to our data and ML practitioners. The goal was not simply to place a model in front of a large collection of logs. We needed bounded extraction, predictable evaluation inputs, responsive product behavior, and quality checks that could follow the system from local development through production. Those requirements shaped every layer of the design, which we will discuss in this blog. Pensive AI wraps AI around deterministic processes, which gives broader coverage, low latency, controlled AI costs, and easier maintenance across the software development lifecycle. Building on this foundation, we plan to explore more agentic debugging experiences, as Part 6 describes.
Early results are encouraging. AI error extraction now covers 100% of failures, including the failures that legacy Pensive classified as unknown. Failed step attempts where no one used Pensive AI averaged 321% more manual debug-log exploration actions than attempts where someone did (an observational comparison, not a causal claim).
Figure 1. Pensive AI architecture. Always-on error extraction and on-demand debugging complement each other and share log sources, the LLM gateway, tracing, and the cache. Archived logs feed offline evals and release gates.
The two paths complement each other. Error extraction improves an existing capability and is always on. It lets the user of a failed Maestro workload quickly check the parts of the logs that may point to an immediate root cause. It has low latency and low cost, and it can help in a large share of cases. On-demand debugging enables a new capability. It looks at symptoms across the logs and adds the LLM’s own knowledge and reasoning for a deeper analysis, at slightly higher latency and cost. Extraction gives a fast first look at every failure, and on-demand debugging triggered by the user goes deeper when that first look is not enough.
Part 1: Finding the useful errors
Legacy Pensive rules are precise, but each one captures a particular log shape. A simplified rule looks like this:
- name: SparkContainerOOM
logSource: GENIE_STDERR
restartable: false
regex: "Container.*is running beyond physical memory limits.*Killing container"
summary: Spark AM container runs out of memory
With Pensive AI, we wanted to find useful errors that had no corresponding rule and adapt more easily when familiar errors changed shape after a platform upgrade. Data Portal (our UI for data pipelines) surfaces these extracted errors when available and links back to the source logs, giving practitioners a focused starting point for triage. That raises a question: how can we ask a model to identify an error without asking it to repeat a long stack trace token by token?
Producing output tokens is much slower than reading input tokens. A direct transcription approach would make long errors expensive and slow. Instead, Pensive numbers the lines of each log and gives the model a sequence of {lineNumber, text} records. The model identifies the first and last lines of the error span, and Pensive reconstructs the selected text from its own log copy, leading to lower cost and better latency. This way, the model always returns two integers (start and end line number), whether the selected logs span a few lines or hundreds of lines. The displayed content comes directly from the original log, reducing hallucinations. The model can still choose the wrong range, which is why extraction quality remains an integral measurement for our AI evals, as we will discuss later.
For orchestrated workflows, “Pensive AI Error Extraction” runs automatically whenever a step fails. A step attempt is one execution of a step within a Maestro workflow. Maestro already calls Pensive for a regex-derived error and restartability classification, so AI extraction runs in the same request and returns its results alongside the established fields. The overall Pensive response must return within Maestro’s hard 90-second post-processing timeout for a failed step attempt.
Figure 2. Error extraction. Legacy rules always run. The AI call is bound by a shared deadline, and late calls are excluded. Pensive merges both results into one response and caches it.
That deadline shaped the extraction path. Pensive extracts errors from the logs in parallel to reduce latency, and the per-log calls share one deadline set well inside Maestro’s timeout limit. A per-log extraction call that misses the deadline is excluded from the result, allowing the overall request to return on time.
The data contract between Pensive AI and the various consumers needed the same care. The legacy data model contained one flattened error string; AI extraction instead returns a list of errors, one for each log source, with deep links back to the originating logs. Changing the old field in place would have broken existing clients. We introduced the new data model beside the legacy non-AI error extraction data model and continued producing both. Data Portal, our user interface for monitoring and observing data pipelines, preferred AI errors when available and fell back to the legacy value when they were not during the rollout. That allowed a gradual rollout and ensured that historical failures still display an error, since we chose not to backfill the old data due to log retention issues.
The migration is still in progress today. The Data Portal UI surface used for failed Maestro steps reads the new AI extracted error field today, while the query editor (for editing and running SQL), Workbench notebooks (managed compute platform and UI to edit and run jupyter based notebooks) and some slack clients calling Pensive still use the legacy error extraction path. Each client needs a compatible schema change before it can consume the new data. Keeping both fields populated lets teams adopt the new behavior at their own pace without forcing a coordinated cutover as we continue evolving Pensive AI.
Part 2: Full failure diagnosis and the product experience
Beyond error extraction, we built Pensive AI Debugging, a tool that analyzes failed step attempts and provides root-cause analysis and suggested remediations. It is available through programmatic APIs, MCP, and the product UI (Data Portal), all backed by a common entry point across the Netflix Data Platform. This shared model supports consistent behavior and custom product experiences.
This diagnosis still has to arrive quickly and remain consistent across investigations. A debugging response can take tens of seconds or a minute to generate, compared with a few seconds for error extraction. We run full AI-based debugging on demand instead of automatically, which keeps costs under control because most failed steps are never opened. We treat the failed step attempt, not the person who triggered it, as the unit of work, so everyone investigating the same failed attempt sees the same diagnosis.
That choice gives us a stable unit of work for caching. We cache each debugging response by step attempt. A second request becomes a key-value read instead of another AI inference call. The cache also prevents duplicate work, reducing latency and lowering costs further. This also means that a debugging generated in the Data Portal is cached and immediately retrieved for the MCP path instead of incurring another AI inference call. A conditional write creates an in-progress record, one caller starts generation, and other callers wait for the shared result to avoid conflicts when concurrent requests come in for the same step attempt failure. If generation remains in progress past an abandonment timeout, Pensive treats the record as abandoned and reclaims it. Completed responses expire after 90 days to help control costs and optimize storage because debugging requests for much older workloads are uncommon.
Pensive AI supports multiple ways to initiate debugging responses. A caller can (1) read a cached response, (2) generate one if no cache entry exists, or (3) regenerate and overwrite an existing response. Those semantics support the product UI, programmatic access, and the evaluation harness while keeping the response associated with a single immutable workload failure.
Figure 3. On-demand debugging. Three client actions share one entry point. A conditional write claims the step attempt. A cache hit returns the cached result. A won claim generates and streams a response, and the result persists even if the client disconnects.
For users, the most important behavior is that a long-running answer feels alive. Pensive streams the response as it is produced. The service emits server-sent events, and the GraphQL layer republishes them as a WebSocket subscription for the Data Portal client.
Each event carries the complete response generated so far. That duplicates a small amount of text, but it keeps the client simple: it does not need a replay buffer or token reassembly logic, and the next event corrects the display after a dropped or late event. Generation is independent of the connection that requested it. A disconnect does not cancel the work, and the final answer still reaches the cache. A hard reload can show a loading state and poll for the completed result. Within the single-page application backing the Data Portal UI, active streams are maintained independently of view and component lifecycle, so navigation does not interrupt a response in progress.
Part 3: Measuring and improving the behavior we want
LLM-assisted systems need more than a demo or a few working examples. Before shipping in production, we need confidence in both error extraction and debugging guidance, and we need to know that we have not regressed on failures that legacy Pensive already handled. We built separate evaluation frameworks focused on the two distinct jobs.
Building labeled data is often the expensive part of evaluation. For error extraction, legacy Pensive’s hand-written rules provide reference labels for failures they recognize. They also serve as excellent ground truth in most cases. We run those rules over production logs and compare their extracted spans with Pensive AI’s output. This gives us a reliable regression set without relabeling every example by hand, though it is not an absolute ground truth (since our human-built rules could also have been stale). For now, we keep these rules frozen as a label source. This lets us continue to build comparison evals and run them on top of the existing system.
Stable inputs are essential for repeatable evaluation experiments where we A/B test new models/configurations or context injections to improve response quality. The logs Pensive AI uses can expire after as few as seven days or as many as 30 days. Production Pensive AI requests archive fetched logs to S3 object storage asynchronously during workload execution time so the upload is not on the user-facing critical path. Uploads do not overwrite an existing object, preserving the exact snapshot used to create an evaluation case. Evals use those archived logs, so score changes remain attributable to the system under test. The archive also prevents parallel experiments from overloading the source systems and lets us run them without affecting production. Cached S3 log inputs further reduce costs when running evaluations.
Concretely, we measure four complementary signals for error extraction:

Inclusion: An LLM judge compares the legacy Pensive error for a failure with the errors Pensive AI extracted and determines whether the known error is still represented, even when wording differs.
Precision: A second judge sees only the extracted AI errors and evaluates whether each is meaningful and actionable on its own.
Repeated noise: A script looks across the whole dataset for lines that recur too often. A generic status line may look harmless in one answer but become distracting if it appears in a large share of failures. Lines appearing in more than about 30% of workflows are candidates for explicit exclusion. In practice, the exclusion list has only three lines, each of which otherwise appeared in nearly every extracted error.
Latency: We record the latency of every extraction call. Quality scores alone cannot reveal when an apparent improvement requires too much additional work, which often correlates with increased AI costs.

This combination gives us an actionable feedback loop. Prompt changes can reduce general noise, while the dataset-level view exposes the stubborn boilerplate that prompt changes do not eliminate. Existing rules act as a regression floor, and archived logs give us a repeatable way to compare changes. At Pensive AI’s scale, model and system choices must satisfy quality, latency, maintainability and cost constraints together.
To seed the debugging ground-truth dataset for evaluation, we mine internal engineering-support Slack threads and use an LLM to identify threads that link to an orchestrated workflow, describe a resolved problem, and match the class of issue Pensive AI handles. A second model synthesizes a reference debugging response from the relevant discussion. Paired with logs from that workflow failure, it becomes a concrete evaluation row in our evals dataset. This approach works only retrospectively, because Pensive AI in production aims to provide debugging guidance before such a Slack discussion happens.
We also made the debugging generation process visible. Tracing follows the request through Pensive, with child spans for each log fetch and extraction tool call. Our tracing backend based on Braintrust brings the prompt, completion, tool calls, and latency into a single view. During early product development, that visibility helped us inspect low-performing debugging responses in context instead of guessing which input or operation caused them. Tracing helped us improve the responses and fill context gaps even before we had comprehensive evals. In production, the API and UI return the trace identifier with the response, so feedback can lead directly to the trace for in-depth analysis.
Part 4: Keeping quality in the release path
Evaluation is not only for experiments with LLM orchestration, models, prompts, or context changes. Changes to log selection, trimming logic, or a source system can change what the model sees and therefore change extraction quality. We use the same evaluation harness and evaluators throughout local development and Pensive AI deployment so those effects are visible before users encounter them.
For each pull request, the code branch is deployed to an isolated preview environment and a CI job runs an experiment with our evals against that isolated environment. Precision and inclusion thresholds gate the merge. The job also runs after a build is promoted, catching interactions that were not present when individual pull requests were evaluated in isolation. If the promoted build misses its thresholds, it alerts the on-call engineer to investigate or roll back.
The evaluator runs on a schedule against production to surface gradual drift or external changes. Developers can also trigger evaluation experiments remotely while iterating, using the same deployed-environment path as CI. Consistent infrastructure makes the results comparable across local iteration, preview builds, promoted builds, and production.
Part 5: Looking for feedback signal from users
The system is only valuable if it reduces the amount of manual debugging and log chasing done by our users. We wanted a measurement that was available from product telemetry and close to the behavior Pensive AI was designed to change. Manual debug-log exploration became one of the main signals. The Pensive interface already offers links to logs for a failed step attempt. To estimate whether the feature reduced raw-log hunting, we compared failed step attempts where someone interacted with Pensive AI with those where no one did. The second group averaged 321% more manual debug-log exploration actions. This observational comparison does not establish causality or a specific reduction in mean time to resolution, but it suggests that focused diagnosis often allows practitioners to inspect fewer raw logs. Programmatic MCP access also lets teams build operational flows with their terminals or custom agentic experiences around the same diagnosis service.
Another more explicit signal we collect is thumbs up and thumbs down on the debugging response. These feedback signals land directly alongside the internal traces so we can quickly associate feedback to the complete log of inputs/outputs and the path the AI took to arrive at the answer. More importantly, we created an internal business-hours alerting system where each thumbs down response sends us a Slack alert. This was valuable to resolve a lot of rough edges and context gaps initially in the product and is helping us improve the product continuously even today.
Figure 4. Feedback loop. A thumbs up or down joins the exact LLM trace that produced the response, by the same logId stamped during generation. Traces and feedback feed ground truth and eval datasets, and each thumbs down sends a Slack alert during business hours.
Part 6: Future Work building on these foundations
Pensive AI is the foundation for more work that goes beyond diagnosis and recommended remediations. We are exploring “Pensive AI Deepthink,” an opt-in managed agentic experience with higher cost and latency. It builds on the precise, low-latency analysis produced by Pensive AI Debugging and gathers additional context from internal documentation, manuals, past Slack discussions, source code, read-only warehouse queries, and Spark execution details. A routing step directs the investigation to the appropriate skill, such as Spark failures, data-audit failures, or late workflows. This keeps the shared starting point stable and deterministic while allowing the investigation to become more specialized, further improving recall. We are also in talks with the Spark team to leverage Pensive AI responses for failure debugging analysis and A/B comparison for upcoming platform migrations.
We also plan to invest in “Pensive AI Error Classification”. Hard-to-maintain legacy rules also classify failures by restartability and by whether they are platform or user caused. Maestro acts on those labels and changes its retry behavior accordingly like failing fast or tuning the default number of retries (platform errors are tried more than user errors by default). Error classifications must meet a higher bar than error extractions and debugging alone. Moving the majority of the error classifications to AI would let us retire most of the remaining rule-maintenance burden and avoid retrying unknown failures that were unlikely to succeed. For restartability, the costliest error is classifying a recoverable failure as non-restartable, because Maestro will turn a step that could have been recovered into a hard failure, leading to end user alerts and manual remediations. The evaluation framework will need to be tuned around that outcome before AI-enabled classifications can take on those decisions. Equally important, we must avoid retrying non-transient failures that will not succeed, because retries waste compute and delay data pipelines.
Our work on Pensive AI in Data Platform addresses concrete user pain points in debugging, improves maintainability for platform owners, and improves precision and recall for error extraction. Pensive AI extends coverage to failures that legacy Pensive previously classified as unknown. Reliability comes from the system around the AI model calls: bounded error extractions, compatible client data contracts, responsive delivery, reproducible evaluations, caching and tracing, and release controls that keep quality and cost visible as the platform changes.
Part 7: Acknowledgements
This work would not have been possible without our stunning colleagues across Data Platform and our Data Engineering and Analytics partners who provided early feedback. While we cannot name everyone individually, we are deeply grateful for their contributions, which shaped both response quality and the product experience. Special thanks to Adith Swaminathan for advising on evaluations and inference improvements and acting as a thought partner. Thank you to the Orchestration team members, especially Deepak Ramalingam and Malcolm Ramirez for their additional engineering contributions.
For dogfooding and integrating Pensive AI as part of user support, we also thank the engineering support organization (ESO Team). We also thank Abhishek Kapatkar (Data Developer Experiences Team) and Emmie Dong (Data Movement Team) for their feedback to improve the Pensive AI integrations with the rest of the ecosystem. Special thanks to the AI Platform team (Kyle Ahn, Rob Mann) and Braintrust Team for helping with distributed tracing, evals infrastructure and model gateway runtime support.
We also thank Kamran Masood, Ely Spears, Ronald Leung, Anjali Norwood, Prashanth Ramdas, Charles Smith, Harikrishna Menon and other leaders for their constructive feedback and support on the Pensive AI project.
